faq.a: Rarely; most contain pre‑peritoneal fat or omentum. Bowel involvement raises the risk of strangulation.
faq.q: Can a xiphoid hernia contain bowel?

faq.a: No. Small defects (<2 cm) can be closed with primary sutures; mesh is reserved for larger defects when sterility can be ensured.
A fracture is painful on bone palpation, shows a step‑off on X‑ray, and lacks a reducible mass.
faq.q: What distinguishes a xiphoid hernia from a sternal fracture?

exam: What bedside manoeuvre helps you decide if the swelling is a hernia or a fracture? — Perform a cough impulse test; a positive impulse suggests a hernia.
A patient with a tender, non‑reducible xiphoid swelling and vomiting presents. What is your next step? — Treat as incarcerated hernia: give IV antibiotics and arrange urgent surgical repair.

How does the management of a small (<2 cm) xiphoid hernia differ from a large one in a low‑resource setting? — Small defects can be closed primarily without mesh; large defects may need mesh if sterility and supplies allow.
Which local condition increases the risk of developing a xiphoid hernia? — Chronic cough from untreated pulmonary TB weakens the anterior abdominal wall.
Why is ultrasound preferred over CT for initial evaluation in this setting? — It is portable, inexpensive, and can identify sac contents and vascularity without radiation.

What are the key features that separate a xiphoid hernia from an epigastric hernia on examination? — Location at the xiphoid tip, attachment to the linea alba, and a positive cough impulse; epigastric hernias are higher and lack these signs.
ai.title: Xiphoid Hernia
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: A xiphoid hernia is a protrusion of soft tissue through a defect in the xiphoid process, usually after trauma or congenital weakness. It presents as a localized, often painful swelling at the lower sternum and may mimic epigastric hernia or sternal fracture.

b: Rare (<1% of ventral hernias) but reported after blunt chest trauma, heavy lifting, or congenital laxity.
More common in males; presentation age 15‑45 years.
Usually solitary; bilateral cases are exceptional.
sections.p: The xiphoid process is the small cartilaginous tip of the sternum that ossifies in adulthood. A defect or rupture allows pre‑peritoneal fat, muscle, or even intra‑abdominal viscera to bulge forward.

b: Xiphoid attaches to rectus abdominis via the linea alba; loss of this support predisposes to herniation.
Hernia sac contents: pre‑peritoneal fat > omentum > small bowel (rare).
Risk factors in low‑resource settings: untreated chest trauma, heavy manual labor, chronic cough (TB), and malnutrition weakening connective tissue.
sections.p: Understanding the anatomy and biomechanics of the xiphoid helps differentiate true hernia from other anterior chest wall swellings.

b: History: recent blunt chest injury, heavy lifting, chronic cough, or congenital awareness of a midline lump.
Examination: firm, reducible swelling at the xiphoid tip; cough impulse may be present; overlying skin may be thin or ulcerated.
Complications: incarceration (pain, non‑reducibility), strangulation (vomiting, peritonitis), ulceration, infection.
When to suspect incarceration: sudden increase in size, constant pain, vomiting, fever.
sections.p: Prompt recognition prevents complications such as incarceration, strangulation, or ulceration of overlying skin.

t.a: Focused physical exam (inspection, palpation, cough impulse)
t.b: Is the swelling reducible? – Reducibility suggests uncomplicated hernia; non‑reducible raises concern for incarceration.
What is the content and is there blood flow? – Shows fat vs. bowel and assesses for compromised perfusion.
Is there a fracture of the xiphoid or underlying rib? – Differentiates hernia from fracture or osteomyelitis.

b: Distinguish from epigastric hernia: epigastric lies above the umbilicus, not attached to the xiphoid; cough impulse often absent.
Distinguish from sternal fracture: fracture is painful on palpation of bone, no reducible mass, and may show step-off on X‑ray.
Management hierarchy: analgesia → imaging (if possible) → surgical referral; emergency surgery only if signs of incarceration/strangulation.
sections.p: Examiners love to test your ability to differentiate this rare hernia from more common anterior chest wall problems and to plan management with limited resources.

b: Analgesia: paracetamol ± NSAID (if no renal or ulcer risk).
If incarcerated: give broad‑spectrum IV antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) and arrange urgent herniorrhaphy.
Elective repair: primary suture repair of the defect; mesh only if size >2 cm and sterile environment available.
Post‑op care: wound inspection, pain control, early ambulation; advise avoidance of heavy lifting for 6 weeks.
sections.p: Treatment is surgical repair; however, initial steps focus on stabilisation and assessment in low‑resource settings.

b: Assuming all anterior chest wall swellings are epigastric hernias – miss the need for xiphoid‑specific repair.
Ordering CT when portable ultrasound would suffice – waste of scarce resources.
Delaying surgery in a non‑reducible mass – risk of strangulation.
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from misidentifying the lesion or over‑investigating.

ai.clinicalScope: Xiphoid (xiphisternum) hernia in adolescents and adults presenting to low‑resource hospitals in East Africa
whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in size, severe pain, vomiting, fever, or signs of bowel obstruction – treat as surgical emergency.
